_about: Settings for the metadata score (stages/metadata_score.py). Every number here is either a platform rule, a published cut-off, or a model choice; each carries its provenance below. Values learned from the corpus are NOT stored here - they are computed from the export and cached.

_provenance.fields.*.length: Only limits a published external source states. title: at most 150 characters not counting spaces - EIP-AGRI Common Format (European Commission, 2015): project title 'short and easily understandable (one key sentence on the project; max 150 characters, word count – no spaces)'. description: 50 to 5,000 characters - Google Search Central, Dataset structured data: 'The summary must be between 50 and 5000 characters long'. subtitle and keywords: no published source gives a length or a count, so none is imposed and the length sub-pillar is not evaluated for them. Earlier ranges (title 5-12 words, description 40-80 words, keywords 4-10) came from an LLM prompt and were removed.
_provenance.fields.*.weight: Equal weights, what most composite indicators use (OECD/JRC Handbook on Constructing Composite Indicators, 2008: 'Most composite indicators rely on equal weighting'). Every field is expected, subtitle included: an empty field scores 0 on the field score and on each pillar, and counts in the KO score, as in Ochoa & Duval's (2006) completeness metric, which counts the fields that hold a value, so a missing field adds nothing to the score. (Until version 7 an empty subtitle was left out and the remaining weights renormalised.)
_provenance.pillars: Equal weights, same source, over four pillars: structural, semantic and functional (measured, following the 2025 KO quality diagram) and llm (an LLM's 0-100 score of the field; version 10). The LLM pillar's equal share is a choice: a quarter of every field score.
_provenance.readability: LIX (Bjornsson 1968), applied to newspapers in 11 languages by Bjornsson (1983). On Bjornsson's scale 20 is very easy and 60 very difficult; below 40 covers easy and ordinary prose. Full score at or below 40, zero at or above 60, linear between. Applied to descriptions only, as Ochoa & Duval (2006) apply a readability index to the description, and only from min_words up: readability formulas are defined on samples of about 100 words and are unreliable on fragments; 40 words is a choice: below it one or two sentences dominate the index.
_provenance.models.embedding: Multilingual retrieval model (Wang et al. 2024, multilingual E5). Used for semantic findability, premise selection and term matching across languages.
_provenance.models.nli: XLM-RoBERTa large fine-tuned on MNLI + XNLI: judges whether the content supports a field, in any of the XNLI languages and across languages.
_provenance.reference: What a field is checked against. Choice, not a published rule: source 'summary' checks every field against the KO's summary (ko_content_flat_summarised) only - the text the export's *_llm fields were written from - with English KOs in scope for now (pipeline.py --languages English); a KO without a summary has no reference, and its semantic and functional sub-pillars are not evaluable. Source 'file' checks against the vision model's reading of the file followed by the extracted text (versions up to 8). Measured caveat, June 2026 export, English KOs: the share of a field's words found in the summary favours the export's *_llm fields over the contributor's (titles +0.11, descriptions +0.19), while against the file it does not (-0.02, -0.05), so results are reported as measured against the summary the *_llm fields were written from. Long texts are cut at max_chars, and NLI premises are drawn from the first max_chunks chunks. Version 15 (decided 2026-10-30): with --resummarise the reference is the fresh summary in the document's own language (stages/resummarise.py), so a non-English KO's fields are measured in their own language; its English version is the KO's row in the corpus index and the secondary reference for English-language fields. Without --resummarise nothing changes: the export's summary, English, is the reference. The reference summary is stored with every run (details.jsonl 'summary', the Summaries sheet).
_provenance.coverage: Coverage: the share of the file's key_terms most characteristic words that the field carries, literally or by meaning. Key terms: function words excluded (Zipf >= key_term_max_zipf in any corpus language, i.e. more frequent than 1 in 1,000 words; Zipf scale of van Heuven et al. 2014, frequencies from wordfreq), the rest ranked by TF-IDF (Salton & Buckley 1988) with sublinear tf (Manning, Raghavan & Schutze 2008, 'Sublinear tf scaling'). 10 matches the usual keyphrase evaluation cut-off (F1@10, Meng et al., ACL 2017). 'By meaning' must beat the null_percentile of similarities of null_terms randomly drawn corpus keywords to the same field - a threshold learned per field.
_provenance.bm25: k1 = 1.2, b = 0.75: OpenSearch's defaults (OpenSearch documentation, keyword search), at the edge of the ranges Robertson & Zaragoza (2009) report as reasonably good in many circumstances (1.2 < k1 < 2, 0.5 < b < 0.8).
_provenance.specificity: A word's specificity is the lower of (a) its normalised IDF across all KOs, which marks platform-generic words such as 'agriculture', and (b) 1 - its Zipf frequency / zipf_max in general usage of any language found in the corpus (wordfreq 3.x, Speer 2022), which marks everyday words in every language. Per-language document frequencies were tried first and dropped: only five languages have 200+ KOs, so in the other languages every word looked rare. zipf_max 8 is the top of the Zipf scale ('the' is 7.7).
_provenance.coherence: Coherence between title, description and keywords (Ochoa & Duval 2009, after Bruce & Hillmann's 'logical consistency and coherence'). Similarity is compared with the same field of null_pool randomly drawn KOs, so the score reads as 'better than this share of chance pairings' instead of an uncalibrated cosine.
_provenance.diversity: Keyword diversity follows KPEval (Wu, Yin & Chang, Findings of ACL 2024): the lexical dup_token_ratio after stemming and the semantic emb_sim, the mean pairwise cosine of the keyword embeddings. emb_sim has no natural scale, so it is anchored to the 5th-95th percentile over anchor_sample original keyword sets drawn from the corpus.
_provenance.llm_score: The LLM pillar (choice), stages/llm_score.py: one call per field per version - the KO's summary (max_summary_chars of it), that one field and the criteria of the three measured pillars in; one 0-100 score and a one-sentence reason out. Fields are never batched into one prompt, because multi-field answers were where the output broke. An empty field scores 0 without a call. Rating named criteria with an LLM is the approach of G-Eval (Liu et al., EMNLP 2023); scoring each version on its own removes the position bias Wang et al. (ACL 2024) found in pairwise comparison. Model (choice): glm-5.2 wrote neither version: the contributor wrote one, and the LLM version is written by generate_metadata's model (qwen3.5 by default; before version 12, the export's *_llm fields, written by the platform's qwen3-30b-a3b-awq), so self-preference (Panickssery et al., NeurIPS 2024) cannot favour one; no Qwen model is used as the judge for the same reason, being of the writer's family. Of the two other models measured as judges in version 7, glm-5.2 repeated its verdict more often with the order reversed (60-63% against 55% for gpt-oss-120b), and gpt-oss-120b always reasons and rejects reasoning_effort, so tight answers can come back truncated (../USING_LLMS.md). Known and accepted for now: the G-Eval authors report that LLM evaluators may favour LLM-generated text, i.e. the *_llm version, and in this project's version-7 comparisons LLM judges never once preferred the contributor's version (METHODS.md section 6). Version 12: the prompt names the KO's declared language, says the summary is English, and asks for meaning to be judged across languages without penalising the language itself - LLM evaluators are less reliable on non-English text (Hada et al., Findings of EACL 2024), and the platform is multilingual. The prompt change means version-12 LLM-pillar values are not comparable with version 11's. Version 15: the prompt names the summary's language (the document's own with --resummarise, else English) instead of asserting English.
_provenance.cross_lingual: Version 13 (decided 2026-10-08): a lexical measurement cannot read across languages, so when a field is written in a different language from the reference text (the share of the field's alphabetic tokens that are known words of the reference's language, zipf_frequency >= known_word_zipf in wordfreq, Speer 2022 - open-set langdetect misfires on short fields, reading 'personal development, dairy farming' as French; a field gates when that share is under known_share and it has at least min_tokens tokens; the reference's language is detected fresh from the current reference, so --resummarise overrides carry their own), the purely lexical parts are not evaluable - excluded from their means, never zeroed, the rule every unmeasurable part follows: bm25_findability (the functional pillar is then semantic findability alone, multilingual E5), usefulness.coverage (literal-or-chance, with a chance threshold calibrated on same-language pairs), and consistency.accuracy for keywords (same threshold). The NLI accuracy of title/subtitle/description stays: XNLI is cross-lingual by construction (Conneau et al., EMNLP 2018). Version 14: keywords matching the document-language summary's language are measured against THAT summary instead of abstaining (same literal-or-chance test, chunks and chance threshold from the document-language text; the evidence names the basis) - so keyword faithfulness abstains only when the keywords match neither summary's language. bm25_findability stays not evaluable cross-lingually even with a document-language summary: findability is a corpus property, the corpus is indexed on English summaries, and a query in a language only one KO carries would rank first without competition - a fake number. usefulness.coverage also stays not evaluable: key-term extraction needs document-frequency and word-frequency statistics in the field's language, which a single secondary summary does not provide. A version whose faithfulness is not evaluable passes the recommendation guard - a measurement gap, not a verdict. min_tokens 2, known_word_zipf 2.0 and known_share 0.5 are choices. Scores of non-English fields are not comparable with version 12. Version 15: with --resummarise the reference is in the document's language, so a same-language field is measured on every lexical part; bm25_findability is now gated on the CORPUS INDEX's language (the export's English summaries, CorpusIndex.corpus_language) rather than the reference's, for the same reason as before - a query in a language only this KO's row carries would rank first without competition - which is the same rule while the reference is English. usefulness.coverage runs on the document-language reference: its key terms come from the reference with the reference's own language added to the stopword filter (key_terms extra_langs), so a language few corpus KOs share does not yield function words. The English version of the summary replaces version 14's document-language secondary reference: keywords written in English on a non-English document are measured against it (_summary_en, KOContext.alt_*). The keyword diversity stemmer follows the reference's language. Scores of non-English KOs under --resummarise are not comparable with version 14.
_provenance.recommendation: A version other than the contributor's is recommended for a field only if its field score is higher and its accuracy against the reference text (consistency) is not lower than the contributor's by more than accuracy_tolerance: optimising a proxy degrades the true objective (Gao, Schulman & Hilton, ICML 2023). The tolerance 0.02 is a choice.
_provenance.llm_score.per_criterion: Version 11 (choice): the same call also returns the LLM's own 0-100 reading of each measured pillar's criteria (structural, semantic, functional), reported next to the measured values so every pillar has two sources - code and LLM - whose agreement is summarised per run (Spearman, stages/analysis.llm_agreement). Rating named aspects separately is G-Eval's form-filling design (Liu et al., EMNLP 2023). Only the overall score enters the field score; the per-criterion numbers are reported, never scored. The prompt change means version-11 LLM-pillar values are not comparable with version 10's.
_provenance.summary_check: Version 11, reported and never scored, like the content report: the reference summary is the pipeline's instrument, so its quality is read out rather than folded into the score. Compression = summary words / file words; no published universal ratio exists, so no absolute threshold is imposed - the run's own p5-p95 flags outliers, the learned-from-the-corpus principle the density anchors use. Key-term coverage reuses the coverage machinery (TF-IDF key terms of the file, literal match). NLI support follows the bidirectional-NLI design of summary_evaluation/03: sampled summary sentences as hypotheses, their best-matching file chunks (reference.chunk_words, reference.premises_per_hypothesis) as premises, mean P(entailment). sentences = 6 is a choice: enough to spread over a long summary at a few NLI pairs per KO. A summary detected as non-English is flagged because the platform writes summaries in English by design. Version 13: the percentile thresholds are anchored WITHIN each file-language group of at least 30 checked KOs (falling back to run-wide below that, each check recording its anchor), because cross-lingual readings - an English summary against a non-English file - run systematically lower (measured: NLI support ~0.5 cross-lingual vs ~0.8 same-language), and a run-wide percentile would flag non-English KOs for being non-English. Version 15: the language flag becomes summary_language_mismatch - the detected language against the one the summary is meant to be in (the document's own with --resummarise, summary_language_expected; else English) - since summaries are no longer English by design.
_provenance.resummarise: Version 15 (decided 2026-10-30; opt-in via --resummarise, never the default): the reference summary is written in the document's own language (summary_language 'document': the KO's language, read from the file itself; an English document gets English) and becomes the reference every field of that KO is measured against; an English version of it (one translation call for a non-English document, none for an English one; translate_to_english) replaces the KO's own row in the corpus index, which stays English like every other row (CorpusIndex.override_reference), and serves as the secondary reference for English-language fields on a non-English document. The file is read as it is, with no page cap (max_pages 0): a PDF or image as page images, one page per image at render_dpi (no stacking); an office document (doc/docx/ppt/pptx/xls/xlsx/odt/odp/ods/rtf) converted to PDF by LibreOffice headless first (office_convert_timeout); a video or audio file downloaded (max_file_mb 600, download_timeout 300), its sound transcribed by whisper-large-v3 (transcription_model; Radford et al., ICML 2023: 'When scaled to 680,000 hours of multilingual and multitask supervision, the resulting models generalize well to standard benchmarks and are often competitive with prior fully supervised results but in a zero-shot transfer setting without the need for any fine-tuning') in pieces of audio_segment_seconds, and video_frames frames sampled evenly across a video (frame_width wide) shown next to the transcript. A document with more than chunk_pages pages (12, the provider's images-per-prompt limit, max_images_per_call) is summarised by hierarchical merging (Chang, Lo, Goyal & Iyyer, ICLR 2024, BooookScore, which studies 'two prompting workflows: (1) hierarchically merging chunk-level summaries, and (2) incrementally updating a running summary' and finds 'Incremental updating yields lower BooookScore but higher level of detail than hierarchical merging'): detailed notes per chunk of pages, merged merge_fanin at a time until one summary remains - coherence chosen over the extra detail. Every draft is then verified against its source (verify true), following Chain-of-Verification (Dhuliawala et al., Findings of ACL 2024: the model 'first (i) drafts an initial response; then (ii) plans verification questions to fact-check its draft; (iii) answers those questions independently so the answers are not biased by other responses; and (iv) generates its final verified response'), adapted: one call per chunk reads the draft against those pages and lists statements they contradict and major content they lack, and one revision call applies the findings - no revision call when nothing was found. Calls per KO: 2-4 for a document of up to chunk_pages pages, about two more per further chunk plus the merges; one transcription call per audio segment. The platform's summary is kept (_summary_platform); the basis, kind, pages, chunks, calls and findings are recorded per KO (_resummarised_from), and the summary, its English version and the platform's are written to details.jsonl and the Summaries sheet. A KO whose file cannot be fetched or read falls back to the export's text (basis export_text), and a failed file flow retries once from the export's text. The prompt keeps the platform summariser's brief (every major topic, entities and numbers preserved, proportional length). Runs with --resummarise are not comparable with runs on the export's summaries, nor with version-14 runs (English reference). Earlier versions: 11 (opt-in regeneration from the export's text), 12 (the file downloaded and shown as it is, at most 50 pages stacked into 12 tiles, one call, no map-reduce - a cap set 2026-10-08 and lifted 2026-10-30), 14 (an extra document-language summary as a secondary reference, superseded by this version). The provider rejects PDFs sent natively, so pages-as-images is the delivery (verified 2026-10-08); 12 images per prompt is its measured limit (2026-10-09); /v1/audio/transcriptions with whisper-large-v3 verified 2026-10-30. render_dpi 120, render_jpeg_quality 80, max_tokens 4000, merge_fanin 8, video_frames 12, frame_width 1024, audio_segment_seconds 600 and office_convert_timeout 180 are choices.
_provenance.generate_metadata: Version 12 (choice), on by default, off with --use-existing-llm: the LLM variant of the four fields is written fresh from the reference summary by the currently served model (model '' = the default client, qwen3.5 at the time of writing), one call per KO, instead of reading the *_llm fields the platform's older improver left in the export - the comparison becomes the contributor against a current model, and with --resummarise both the summary and the fields are the current model's. Generation is blind: the model sees the summary and the published field rules only, never the contributor's fields, so the LLM version is an independent rewrite; the rules in the prompt are the same published limits the structural pillar measures, so writer and scorer share one yardstick. Each field is written in the document's own language (rule of 2026-10-08): file_language read from the pages during --resummarise, else the detected language of the stored text, never the contributor's declared languages; the input summary stays English, and the judge is told the language and not to penalise it (llm_score). Until then the fields were written in British English - scores across that change are not comparable. The generator must be a different model from the judge (self-preference, Panickssery et al., NeurIPS 2024); the pipeline warns when they match. max_summary_chars 24000 and max_tokens 2000 are choices; at most 10 keywords in the brief is a choice (2026-10-08) - the count is never scored. A KO whose summary is empty or whose call fails keeps the export's fields and is marked per KO. Version-12 llm columns are not comparable with earlier runs (a different author wrote the fields). Version 15: the prompt names the summary's language (the document's own with --resummarise, else English) instead of asserting English, so the fields and the summary are in one language on a re-summarised non-English KO.
_provenance.title_rules: A title that is an internal project code (D3.1, T2.3, WP2, 'Task 4') or a file name is not 'short and easily understandable' to its reader (EIP-AGRI Common Format) nor 'descriptive' (Google Search Central, title links: 'Write descriptive and concise text... Avoid vague descriptors'). Checked in completeness; the file name is compared with ko_object_name. The description field is stored as editor HTML, so it is converted to text before any check instead of being counted as noise.
